## My request:
Run the material mapping and try to create a CPU hot-spot analysis, where most of the time is spent, particularly if this a specific detector part that sticks out

I’ll run the material recording and mapping workflow, then profile it to separate geometry setup, transport, mapping, and output costs. I’ll also check whether any detector region accounts for a disproportionate amount of the work.

The preflight again reports changed environment fingerprints and no verified full DD4hep/Geant4 source trees. I’ll use the installed runtime and available ACTS source, verify them directly, and keep the detector inputs unchanged.

The installed ACTS mapper can use the native Gen3 surfaces directly. I’ll start with a diagnostic map and report its sampling coverage. For detector attribution, I’ll compare controlled runs that remove selected detector subtrees; those timings will be kept separate from material-step counts, which alone do not measure CPU time.

Another task I have for you:

- I want a stacked histogram plot of t_X0 (y-axis) vs eta (x-axis) where the single components for the sub-detectors are shown one above another, make a few variations in granularity
  - beampipe, pixels, shorts, strips, long strips
  - same, but pixels, short strip, long strips sub-divided into silicon, rest of module(=module-silicon), cabling, cooling, support (staves + fixture)
- Make this as a script that it can be re-run on several layouts

I’ll add a reusable material-budget plotter to this work. It will show stacked mean \(t/X_0\) versus \(\eta\), both by subsystem and by silicon, module remainder, cabling, cooling, and support. I’ll verify how the recorded material steps can be attributed to those categories.

The recorder is now transporting tracks through the full model. For the detailed stacks, I can match each material step to its DD4hep volume and component role. The service volumes contain effective cable-and-cooling mixtures, so I’ll split those using their constituent radiation-length contributions and check that every stack still sums to the recorded total.

The first profile shows a clear hotspot: Geant4 repeatedly scans the volume tree to rebuild production-cut tables between events. That scan dominates the sampled stacks, while transport takes much less time. I’ll test larger track batches to measure that overhead separately, and use the larger sample for the material-budget plots.

The 10,000-track recording completed successfully. Its event phase took 68 seconds, compared with 143 seconds for 2,000 tracks in smaller batches. That supports the finding that repeated initialization is expensive. The plotter now has subsystem, barrel/endcap, and detailed component views; I’m checking its attribution and material sums before rendering them.

The Gen3 material map completed, including the per-subsystem timing runs. The full mapping algorithm took about 6.9 seconds for 10,000 tracks, much less than recording. The attribution check stopped on a material step whose computed midpoint landed in the world volume; I’m resolving that mismatch before accepting the stacked plots.

The mismatch comes from a tiny step that is shorter than the precision of its stored float coordinates at a volume boundary. I’ve added a recovery confined to that float-rounding interval; it requires an unambiguous component and material match. The plotter’s tests pass, including zero-crossing normalization, additive stacks, and mixture splitting.

All 1.81 million recorded material steps now have an attribution, and the stacks reproduce each track’s total within float precision. Only one tiny step needed the boundary-rounding recovery. The plots show substantial service-material peaks: short-strip cabling near \(|\eta|\approx2.1\), and pixel services near \(|\eta|\approx3\). I’m retaining those features in the plots and report.

The timing controls identify the short-strip barrel as the strongest recording-cost contributor: removing it reduced event-phase CPU from 50 to 27 seconds for the same diagnostic workload. The costs are not additive—removing the short-strip endcap increased runtime in one test. I’m checking that result and keeping these timings distinct from material-step counts.

The reusable runner now passes an end-to-end replay and produces SVG, PDF, PNG, and histogram JSON, with 40- and 80-bin signed-\(\eta\) views plus a folded-\(|\eta|\) view. The map accounts for all recorded steps, but 14.7% of its targets remain unpopulated. I’ll keep that sampling limit explicit in the report.

The repeated controls confirm the short-strip barrel gives the largest recording reduction, though the gain varies from 27% to 46%. The earlier short-endcap slowdown did not repeat. The largest mapping subset is the long-strip barrel; mapping time is mainly spent testing every candidate surface. I’m finishing the report and validation now.

Done. I ran **10,000 geantinos** through the current BeamPipe + Tracker model and created the reusable plotter.

The outputs include subsystem, barrel/endcap, and detailed component stacks, with **40/80 signed-\(\eta\) bins** and folded \(|\eta|\). Each stack shows mean \(t/X_0\) per incident track.

![Subsystem material budget]([redacted]

![Detailed component material budget]([redacted]

The service peaks are substantial: short-strip cabling dominates near \(|\eta|\approx2.1\), pixel services near \(|\eta|\approx3\). Sensor silicon includes guards; ASICs belong to module remainder.

Use [run.py]([redacted] in the activated ACTS environment. The [instructions]([redacted] cover fresh recordings, existing recordings, and alternate layouts through `--build-dir`. Outputs are SVG, PDF, PNG and histogram JSON. Five tests and the complete replay passed.

The CPU analysis found repeated **Geant4 material/cuts-tree initialization** dominates recording. Short-strip-barrel removal reduced event CPU by **27–46%** in diagnostic controls. Mapping is dominated by surface-intersection tests, with the long-strip barrel the largest subset. The map remains diagnostic: **14.7% of targets are unpopulated**.

[Full results, plots and CPU measurements]([redacted] Detector inputs are unchanged; logger and dashboard validation passed.
